You probably don't use the site anymore since the question was asked a year ago, but I'll post an answer anyway because it was a good problem and there's an ever so slight chance someone else will take a look at this. 
 Before I solve this, let me get some nomenclature/assumptions of my own out of the way: 
 
 Instead of $\theta$ being the separating angle for the two spherical caps, let it be $\alpha$. 
 When I refer to the central axis of a spherical cap (SC) I imply the axis which intersects the center of the SC's base and the center of our sphere. 
 I'll assume none of the SCs are larger than hemispheres. 
 I'll assume the SCs intersect. 
 
 Therefore, the farthest any point from the intersection of the two SCs from the center of the SC can only be $\Delta\phi = \pi/2$, using the spherical coordinate system. 
 The problem states that there is are two SCs with base radii $a_1$ and $a_2$ on a sphere of radius $r$ with an angle of $\alpha$ between the central axes of the two SCs. 
 As you mentioned, the angle between the SC's central axis and a radius from the center of the sphere to the circumference of the SC's base are $\Phi_1 = \arcsin(a_1/r)$ and $\Phi_2 = \arcsin(a_2/r)$. 
 Align the sphere such that SC-1's central axis and the $x$-axis are parallel (in the $\mathbb{R^3}$ coordinate system).  Translate the sphere to the origin.  Rotate the sphere such that the central axis of SC-2 is on the $xz$-plane.  Angle $\alpha$ now rises from the $x$-axis towards the $z$-axis.  Angle $\Phi_2$ is contained in $\alpha$ in the same plane, rising in the same direction (but not starting from the $x$-axis).  These actions are legal since they don't distort the shape or its surface area. 
 Now that somewhat rigidly defined our problem we can approach it. 
 Let the space curve which defines the intersection of the SC-2's base with the sphere be $\vec s_2(t)$. After some (read: a lot of) vector arithmetic and trigonometry, we arrive at $\vec s_2(t)$.
$$
\vec s_2(t) = \left\{\sqrt{r^2-a_2^2}\cos\alpha+r\cos(\alpha-\Phi_2)\cos t, a_2\sin t, z_2(t)\right\}
$$
for $0\le t\le 2\pi$.  This expression of $\vec s_2(t)$ allows us to project onto the $xy$-plane.  The projection of this base-sphere intersection looks is an ellipse.
The parametrization of the space curve $\vec s_1(t)$ is a bit easier because of the way we set our axes up.
$$
\vec s_1(t)=\left\{\sqrt{r^2-a_1^2},a_1\sin t, a_1\cos t\right\}
$$
When projected onto the $xy$-axis this looks like a line segment.  Using the two projected space curves, I can find the angular limits for $\theta$ in the spherical coordinate system for 3D by finding the intersection of the ellipse and the line segment.
$$
\theta_0=\arccos\frac{\sqrt{r^2-a_1^2}}{r^2-a_1^2+(a_2\sin\arccos\frac{\sqrt{r^2-a_1^2}-\sqrt{r^2-a_2^2}\cos\alpha}{r\cos(\alpha-\Phi_2)})^2}
$$
It's messy, but it's a constant at least!  We know that for the surface area we are interested in is for values of $\theta$ such that $-\theta_0\le \theta\le\theta_0$ 
 Now we need to find the angular limits for $\phi$ in our spherical coordinate system.  These we know to change over $\theta$ since you can imagine that as we rotate our sphere along the $z$-axis the area of interest's width changes (the angle from the $z$-axis to the position vectors of the surface area we're looking at changes). 
 For the top limit of $\phi$, we look at the bottom spherical cap's surface along the sphere.  We use the parametrization I provided earlier.  Since $z_1(t) =  a_1cos(t)$ and $t$ is analogous to $\theta$ in my parametrization, I can use $\cos \phi = \frac{z}{r}$ to find that 
$$
\phi_1(\theta) = \arccos\frac{a_1\cos\theta}{r}
$$
Similarly, using 
$$
z_2(t)=r\sin(\alpha-\Phi_2)+a_2(1-\cos t)\sin(\arcsin(\frac{r}{a_2}\sin\Phi_2)+\alpha)
$$
which I didn't post at $\vec s_2(t)$ because of spatial concerns, I can find
$$
\phi_1(\theta)  = \arccos\frac{z_2(\theta)}{r}
$$
Thus, for the surface area $A$ of the intersection of two spherical caps $\Sigma$, 
$$
A=\int\int_\Sigma dS=\int_{-\theta_0}^{\theta_0}\int_{\phi_2(\theta)}^{\phi_1(\theta)}(r^2 \sin\phi) d\phi d\theta
$$
I'll be first to admit this integral is probably only numerically solvable, but I couldn't find any elegant geometric approaches to this, so I went with the "brute force" method. 
 EDIT 
 Thanks to Christian Blatter's answer to this question, I can answer in a more concise manner. 
 If I take our sphere situated on the origin as described before, and rotate it in the positive direction about $\hat j$ until $\alpha$ is centered on the $z$-axis, then I say: 
 
 Project space curves $s_1(t)$ and $s_2(t)$ onto the $xy$-plane. 
 Said curves must be ellipses or circles, since the extreme case $\alpha=\pi$ is the only one which yields straight lines upon projection and the answer to that scenario is that the surface area $A=0$. 
 
 If an ellipse is contained within another, then the surface area can be found using the formula for finding the external surface area of a spherical cap (see Christian's answer). 
 If the ellipses intersect at two points (they cannot intersect in this case in three or four), then using the answer to the aforementioned question, we can set up a surface integral for the calculation of $A$, given that the intersection of the ellipses on the $xy$-plane can be described by the two inequalities $a\le u\le b$ and $g(u)\le v\le f(u)$ such that $\left\{a,b:a,b\in\mathbb{R}\land a<b\right\}$, $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, $g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$, and $f(u)>g(u)$ over $u:[a, b]$. 
 Let $x=\frac{u}{\sqrt{r_x}}+c_x$ and $y=v$, for $r_x$ being the semi-diameter in the $x$ direction and $c_x$ being the horizontal shift from the origin to the center of the ellipse from the projection of $s_2(t)$ onto the $xy$-plane. 
 Let $\vec F=\{x, y,\sqrt{r^2-x^2-y^2}\}$, the position vector.
$$
A=\int\int_\Sigma dS=\int_{u=a}^b\int_{v=f(u)}^{g(u)}\left\|\frac{\partial\vec F}{\partial v}\times\frac{\partial\vec F}{\partial u}\right\|dvdu
$$

The formula for the area is complicated (see other answers), but it has a simple Legendre expansion
 $$
A(\theta) = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} a_l P_l(\cos\theta)
$$ 
with coefficients given by the associated Legendre functions,
 $$
a_l = \pi \, (2l+1) \sin(\alpha_1) \sin(\alpha_2) \, P_l^{-1}(\cos\alpha_1) \, P_l^{-1}(\cos\alpha_2)
$$ 
which may be helpful.

 Given the coordinates of the four points, obtain the vectors $b_1$, $b_2$, and $b_3$ by vector subtraction. 
 Let me use the nonstandard notation $\langle v \rangle$ to denote $v/\lVert v \rVert$, the unit vector in the direction of the vector $v$. Compute $n_1 = \langle b_1 \times b_2 \rangle$ and $n_2 = \langle b_2 \times b_3 \rangle$, the normal vectors to the planes containing $b_1$ and $b_2$, and $b_2$ and $b_3$ respectively. The angle we seek is the same as the angle between $n_1$ and $n_2$. 
 The three vectors $n_1$, $\langle b_2 \rangle$, and $m_1 := n_1 \times \langle b_2 \rangle$ form an orthonormal frame. Compute the coordinates of $n_2$ in this frame: $x = n_1 \cdot n_2$ and $y = m_1 \cdot n_2$. (You don't need to compute $\langle b_2 \rangle \cdot n_2$ as it should always be zero.) 
 The dihedral angle, with the correct sign, is $\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$. 
 
 (The reason I recommend the two-argument $\operatorname{atan2}$ function to the traditional $\cos^{-1}$ in this case is both because it naturally produces an angle over a range of $2\pi$, and because $\cos^{-1}$ is poorly conditioned when the angle is close to $0$ or $\pm\pi$.)

Assume the transformation from geographic coordinates (latitude, longitude) to image coordinates (x, y) can be modeled as an affine transformation involving rotation, scaling, and translation: z = ρ R_θ w + z₀, where w is the geographic coordinate vector, z is the image coordinate vector, ρ is the scaling factor, R_θ is the rotation matrix, and z₀ is the translation vector.
2. Use the two known pairs (w₁, z₁) and (w₂, z₂) to solve for the unknowns ρ, θ, and z₀:
   a. Compute ρ as the ratio of the Euclidean distances between the image points and the geographic points: ρ = dist(z₁, z₂) / dist(w₁, w₂).
   b. Compute θ as the angle between the vectors (w₂ - w₁) and (z₂ - z₁).
   c. Compute z₀ as z₁ - ρ R_θ w₁.
3. Once ρ, θ, and z₀ are determined, use the formula z = ρ R_θ w + z₀ to map any new geographic coordinate w to its image coordinate z.
4. Apply this method to the sample data, and use the provided Haskell code to perform the calculations for the sample point (37.7, -122.3).

2. Set up a system of linear equations to find a 2x2 transformation matrix A such that A * v = u and A * z = w.
3. Express A as a matrix with unknowns (a, b, c, d), and solve the matrix equation:

I had an interview question a couple days ago involving the calculation of the amount of heavy numbers between in a given range. I came up with a basic solution, which was to iterate over the entire range and test for the heaviness of each number. I realized right away that its a terribly inefficient method of solving the problem. In the interest of educating myself I have been tackling the problem today to try and learn more about this type of problem. Its tough for me, because I don't have a super strong mathematics background but I'm trying to learn. 
 Basically, the problem goes like this: 
 Take any 2 numbers from 0 to 200,000,000. In that range, calculate the number of "heavy numbers". This is calculated by adding together all of the component digits and then dividing by the number of components. If the average is greater than 7, the number is considered heavy. 
 Example: 
 1234: 1+2+3+4/4 = 2.5 (not heavy)
8996: 8+9+9+6/4 = 8 (heavy)
 
 So given the range 1002 - 12089, my naive approach is to iterate over each number between and calculate its weight. This approach quickly falls apart when dealing with very large number ranges. 
 I've done quite a bit of searching via Google and Bing and beyond a couple of posts where people have copy/pasted verbatim the question, I find almost no information about this kind of problem. I suspect that this type of problem is called something other than "heavy numbers" but I'm at a loss as to what that the terminology is.  
 Here is a link to one such discussion:  http://groups.google.com/group/algogeeks/browse_thread/thread/a1b824107afe3801 
 I'm hoping that someone who is familiar with type of scenario can explain alternative ways to solve the problem in a simple manner, and that I might ask follow up questions until I understand. 
 Thanks for reading.
Rq_a: How can one efficiently calculate the number of 'heavy numbers'—numbers whose average digit value exceeds 7—within a large numerical range, such as from 0 to 200,000,000, without resorting to brute-force iteration? What mathematical or algorithmic techniques (such as generating functions or dynamic programming) can be used to solve this problem exactly or approximately, and how can these methods be applied to arbitrary ranges and digit lengths?
Mt_a:
1. Recognize that brute-force iteration is inefficient for large ranges.
2. For numbers of a fixed length (e.g., 5 digits), model the problem using generating functions, where the coefficient of x^k in the expansion represents the count of numbers with digit sum k.
3. To find 'heavy numbers,' sum the coefficients for digit sums that yield an average digit value greater than 7 (i.e., sum > 7 * number of digits).
4. This generating function approach can be implemented via dynamic programming, which counts the number of ways to achieve each possible digit sum for a given length.
5. For arbitrary ranges, decompose the range into manageable subranges (e.g., by digit length or leading digits), and adjust the generating function accordingly.
6. To handle any interval [l, h], compute the count for [0, h] and subtract the count for [0, l-1].
7. For estimation rather than exact calculation, use probabilistic methods such as the Central Limit Theorem or Large Deviation Theory to approximate the distribution of digit sums and estimate the number of heavy numbers.
Ra_a: To efficiently count heavy numbers in a large range, use generating functions or dynamic programming to compute the number of numbers with sufficiently high digit sums for each digit length, breaking the range into subproblems as needed. For approximate answers, probabilistic methods like the Central Limit Theorem can provide estimates.
Rq_b: Where can I find practical, step-by-step implementations of algorithms (such as dynamic programming) to efficiently count 'heavy numbers'—numbers whose average digit value is greater than 7—within a large range, and are there resources or tutorials that explain these solutions in detail?

query: When calculating the $P$ for at least $x$ success one uses $\text{max} (x-1)$ instead, and then take $1- (\text{max} (x-1))$. This works. And I understand it. Because we use the complement to calculate it, because the calculator supports it. But what I do not understand is the following. When calculating a combination of these, $P(\text{max}\,\, x\,\,\, \text{and}\,\,\, \text{min}\,\, y)$ we can just forget about the $1 - (\text{max}\,\, (x-1))$ part, and just use $\text{max}\,(x-1)$ directly. For example: $$P(\text{at least 150 sixes and at most 180 sixes)} = P(\text{max}\,\, 180 \,\,\text{sixes}) - P(\text{max}\,\,149\,\,\text{sixes}).$$ And then we don't have to do the $1-x$ part. Why is this?
Rq_a: Why, when calculating the probability of getting at least a certain number of successes (e.g., at least 150 sixes in 1000 dice rolls), do we use the complement formula $1 - P(\text{max}(x-1))$, but when calculating the probability of getting between two values (e.g., at least 150 and at most 180 sixes), we can simply subtract cumulative probabilities $P(\text{max}(180)) - P(\text{max}(149))$ without using the complement? How do these approaches relate, and why does the subtraction method work for ranges?
Mt_a: First, to find the probability of at least $x$ successes, we use the complement: $P(\text{at least } x) = 1 - P(\text{at most } x-1)$, because the events 'at least $x$' and 'at most $x-1$' are complements. When considering a range, such as 'at least 150 and at most 180', we want the probability that the number of successes is between 150 and 180 inclusive. This is the probability of at most 180 minus the probability of at most 149: $P(\text{at most } 180) - P(\text{at most } 149)$. This works because the cumulative probability up to 180 includes all outcomes up to 180, and subtracting the cumulative probability up to 149 removes all outcomes below 150, leaving only those between 150 and 180. The complement formula is a special case of this subtraction method when the upper bound is the maximum possible number of successes (e.g., 1000 dice, at most 1000 sixes, which is always probability 1).
Ra_a: The subtraction method for probability ranges works because it isolates the desired interval by removing lower outcomes from the cumulative total, and the complement formula for 'at least $x$' is a special case when the upper bound is the maximum possible value.
Rq_b: How does the formula $1 - P(\text{max } x)$ for calculating the probability of at least $x+1$ successes relate to the formula $P(\text{max } M) - P(\text{max } x)$ for calculating the probability of getting between $x+1$ and $M$ successes? Why does the subtraction method suffice for ranges, and what does the '1' represent in the complement formula?
Mt_b: In the formula $1 - P(\text{max } x)$, the '1' represents the probability of achieving the theoretical maximum number of successes or fewer, which is always 1 (since you can't exceed the maximum possible). When the upper bound is less than the theoretical maximum (i.e., $M < \text{max possible}$), the probability of being between $x+1$ and $M$ successes is given by $P(\text{max } M) - P(\text{max } x)$. This subtraction gives the probability of outcomes strictly greater than $x$ and up to $M$, without needing to use the complement, because the cumulative probabilities naturally partition the outcome space.
Ra_b: The subtraction method works for ranges because it directly calculates the probability of being within the specified interval, and the '1' in the complement formula is just the probability of all possible outcomes up to the maximum.

 For example I may want to ask mathematica to integrate $\int{a x} \mathrm{d}x$! How to tell him that $a$ is a constant?
Rq_a: How does Mathematica interpret symbolic variables like $a$ when performing operations such as integration, especially if I do not explicitly specify that $a$ is a constant? What is the correct way to input such expressions to ensure Mathematica treats $a$ as a constant during calculations?
Mt_a: Mathematica, by default, treats any undefined symbol (such as $a$) as a constant when performing symbolic calculations like integration. If you input an expression like Integrate[a x, x], Mathematica assumes $a$ is independent of $x$ and integrates accordingly. However, it is important to use proper syntax: in Mathematica, multiplication is indicated by a space or an asterisk (*), so 'a x' or 'a*x' is correct, while 'ax' would be interpreted as a single variable named 'ax'.
Ra_a: You do not need to explicitly tell Mathematica that $a$ is a constant; by default, it treats undefined symbols as constants in symbolic calculations. Just ensure you use proper syntax, such as Integrate[a x, x], with a space or asterisk for multiplication.
Rq_b: How can I define variables as constants or assign values to them in Mathematica, and how does the type of assignment (integer vs. decimal) affect symbolic differentiation and precision in calculations?
Mt_b: In Mathematica, you can assign values to variables using the ':=' operator. Assigning an integer value (e.g., a := 7) allows for symbolic differentiation, and the variable is treated with infinite precision. Assigning a decimal value (e.g., b := 7.0) makes the variable a machine-precision number. When differentiating expressions involving these variables (e.g., D[a*t, t] or D[b*t, t]), Mathematica returns the assigned value, and the precision of the result depends on whether the variable was assigned an integer or decimal value. The Precision function can be used to check the precision of variables.
Ra_b: Assign values to variables using ':=' in Mathematica. Integer assignments are treated as symbolic and have infinite precision, while decimal assignments are treated as machine-precision numbers. This affects both differentiation results and numerical precision.

 What is the best way to calculate average latitude and longitude?

Rq_a: Given an array of geographical coordinates specified by latitude and longitude, what is the most statistically sound method to compute their average location, considering the spherical nature of the Earth and the issues that arise with averaging circular quantities?
Mt_a: 1. Recognize that latitude and longitude are angular measurements on a sphere, so simple arithmetic means may not be appropriate due to wrap-around and curvature. 2. Convert each latitude (φ_i) and longitude (λ_i) into 3D Cartesian coordinates on a sphere of radius R using the formulas: (R cos φ_i cos λ_i, R cos φ_i sin λ_i, R sin φ_i). 3. Compute the arithmetic mean of the resulting x, y, and z coordinates to obtain a mean point inside the sphere. 4. Convert this mean 3D point back to latitude and longitude using inverse trigonometric functions: latitude = atan2(z̄, sqrt(x̄² + ȳ²)), longitude = atan2(ȳ, x̄). 5. Optionally, assess the dispersion of the original points by calculating the distance of the mean point from the sphere's center, normalized by the radius.
Ra_a: The best way to average geographical coordinates is to convert each latitude and longitude to 3D Cartesian coordinates, average these, and then convert the result back to latitude and longitude. This method accounts for the spherical geometry of the Earth.
Rq_b: Given an array of latitude and longitude pairs representing points on the Earth's surface, how should one properly define and compute their average, considering that these coordinates lie on a sphere (not in flat Euclidean space), and what are the differences between possible averaging methods such as extrinsic and intrinsic means?
Mt_b: 1. Recognize that latitude and longitude represent points on a sphere, so standard Euclidean averaging does not apply. 2. Decide whether to compute the mean latitude and longitude separately (which may not yield a meaningful result) or to compute the mean position on the sphere. 3. Understand that there are two main types of means for circular or spherical data: extrinsic (the centroid projected onto the sphere) and intrinsic (minimizing the sum of squared geodesic distances, i.e., the Fréchet mean). 4. For the extrinsic mean, convert each point to Cartesian coordinates, average them, and project the result back onto the sphere. 5. For the intrinsic mean, minimize the sum of squared angular distances, which may require comparing several candidate points. 6. Both methods have mathematical formulations, and the choice depends on the desired properties of the average.
Ra_b: To properly average latitude and longitude coordinates, use methods from directional statistics: either compute the extrinsic mean by averaging Cartesian coordinates and projecting back to the sphere, or compute the intrinsic mean by minimizing the sum of squared geodesic distances. The choice depends on the context and desired properties of the average.

2. Substitute into the integral: $\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \int \frac{\cos t~dt}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2 t}}$.
3. Simplify $\sqrt{1-\sin^2 t}$ to $\cos t$.
4. The integral becomes $\int \frac{\cos t}{\cos t} dt = \int dt = t + C$.
5. Substitute back $t = \arcsin x$ to write the answer in terms of $x$.
Ra_b: The integral evaluates to $\arcsin x + C$.
output_a:
There is a standard substitution in this sort of situation, namely $x=\sin\theta$,
where we assume $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$.  Then $dx=\cos\theta\, d\theta$, and $\sqrt{1-x^2}=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{\cos^2\theta}=\cos\theta$ since in our interval $\cos$ is non-negative. 
 Thus
$$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}=\int \frac{\cos\theta}{\cos\theta}d\theta=\int d\theta=\theta+C.$$ 
 But $\theta=\arcsin x$. Now it's over. 
 Comment 1 : Regrettably, it is commonplace in solutions not to mention $-\pi/2 \le \theta \le \pi/2$, and it is commonplace to not justify $\sqrt{\cos^2\theta}=\cos\theta$.  So in an integration question, in most calculus courses, the solution would be even shorter. 
 Comment 2 : Note how close this truly standard approach is, in this case, to the suggestion by David Speyer.  The difference is that the calculus teacher would not notice.  The same substitution is used in many other integrals that involve $\sqrt{1-x^2}$, and close relatives can be used for integrals that involve $\sqrt{a-bx^2}$ where $a$ and $b$ are positive.

 $$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \int \frac{\cos t ~dt}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2 t}} = \int \frac{\cos t ~dt}{\cos t} = \int dt = t.$$ 
 By our substition $x=\sin t$  we have  $t=\arcsin x$. 
 Therefore

I read about the SVD theory and its usage for solving Linear Equation System.
I saw many papers mentioning property of the solution yet no proof of it. 
 The Property:
The solution given the Pseudo Inverse ( $ V {\Sigma}^{-1} {U}^{H} $ ) minimizes both the error norm and the solution norm. 
 The minimization of the error norm is easily proved using the Normal Equations ( $ \hat{x} $ is the Least Squares solution iff $ {A}^{H} A \hat{x} = {A}^{H} b $ ). 
 Yet beyond the intuition of $ \hat{x} $ must lie in the Row Space of A hence its norm is minimized I couldn't find a formal proof for that. 
 Moreover, Let's define $ A = U \Sigma {V}^{H} $ then when we calculate its pseudo inverse we we handle $ \Sigma $ with extra care, only reversing its non zero entries. What the formal reasoning for that? 
 Thanks!
Rq_a: Given a linear system $Ax = b$, and knowing that the least-squares solution $\hat{x} = A^+b$ (where $A^+$ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse) minimizes the error norm $\|Ax-b\|$, what is the formal proof that $\hat{x}$ also uniquely minimizes the solution norm $\|x\|$ among all solutions? Additionally, why does the pseudoinverse involve inverting only the nonzero singular values in the SVD $A = U\Sigma V^H$?
Mt_a:
1. Any solution $x$ to $Ax = b$ can be decomposed as $x = u + v$, where $u$ is in the null space of $A$ and $v$ is in its orthogonal complement (the row space of $A$ or column space of $A^*$).
2. The norm $|x|^2 = |u|^2 + |v|^2$, so to minimize $|x|$, $u$ must be zero, meaning the minimal norm solution lies in the orthogonal complement of the null space.
3. Alternatively, using constrained minimization with Lagrange multipliers, minimizing $|x|^2$ subject to $Ax = b$ leads to a solution in the column space of $A^*$.
4. There can be only one solution in the orthogonal complement of the null space, since the difference of two such solutions would be both in the null space and its orthogonal complement, hence zero.
5. The pseudoinverse solution $A^+b$ both solves $Ax = b$ and lies in the column space of $A^*$, thus it is the unique minimal norm solution.
6. In the SVD, only the nonzero entries of $\Sigma$ are inverted in the pseudoinverse to ensure that the operation is well-defined and does not attempt to invert zero (which is undefined).
Ra_a: The pseudoinverse solution $A^+b$ is the unique solution to $Ax = b$ that minimizes the solution norm $\|x\|$, because it lies in the orthogonal complement of the null space of $A$. In the SVD, only nonzero singular values are inverted in $\Sigma$ to avoid division by zero and to ensure the pseudoinverse is properly defined.
Rq_b: For a linear system $\mathbf{A}x = b$, where $\mathbf{A}$ may be rank-deficient, what is the structure of all least-squares solutions, and why does the pseudoinverse $\mathbf{A}^+$ yield the unique solution of minimal norm? Furthermore, how does the SVD structure explain the special handling of the $\Sigma$ matrix in forming the pseudoinverse?
Mt_b:
1. The set of least-squares solutions to $\mathbf{A}x = b$ forms an affine space: $x_{LS} = \mathbf{A}^+b + (I - \mathbf{A}^+\mathbf{A})y$ for arbitrary $y$.
2. The term $\mathbf{A}^+b$ lies in the range (column space) of $\mathbf{A}^*$, while $(I - \mathbf{A}^+\mathbf{A})y$ lies in the null space of $\mathbf{A}$.
3. The norm of any solution is $\|x_{LS}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{A}^+b\|^2 + \|(I - \mathbf{A}^+\mathbf{A})y\|^2$, so the minimal norm is achieved when $y = 0$.
4. Thus, $\mathbf{A}^+b$ is the unique least-squares solution of minimal norm.
5. In the SVD $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^*$, the $\Sigma$ matrix contains singular values, with zeros corresponding to the null space.
6. The pseudoinverse $\mathbf{A}^+ = \mathbf{V}\Sigma^+\mathbf{U}^*$ is constructed by inverting only the nonzero singular values in $\Sigma$; zeros remain zeros to avoid undefined operations and to ensure the pseudoinverse acts only on the range space.
Ra_b: The pseudoinverse $\mathbf{A}^+b$ is the unique least-squares solution of minimal norm because it lies in the range of $\mathbf{A}^*$, and the SVD construction ensures only nonzero singular values are inverted in $\Sigma$ to properly define the pseudoinverse.

As Jack pointed out in a comment, the question is somewhat unclear. I interpret it as follows: 
 You have a system $Ax=b$ of linear equations. You understand why $\hat x=A^+b$, where $A^+$ is the (Moore–Penrose) pseudo-inverse of $A$, minimizes the error norm $|Ax-b|$, but you want to know why, if $Ax=b$ has solutions, $\hat x$ is the unique solution that minimizes the solution norm $|x|$. 
 You state that $\hat x$ must lie in the row space of $A$. That's true in the real case; more generally, in the complex case, $\hat x$ must lie in the column space of $A^*$, or equivalently in the orthogonal complement of the null space of $A$. This can be seen in two different ways: 
 Any solution $x$ of $Ax=b$ can be written as $x=u+v$, where $u$ is in the null space of $A$ and $v$ in its orthogonal complement. Then $|x|^2=|u|^2+|v|^2$. Since $u$ is in the null space of $A$, $v$ also solves $Ax=b$. Thus, the solution with minimal norm must have $u=0$, and must therefore lie in the orthogonal complement of the null space. 
 Alternatively, this can be derived using constrained minimization. To minimize $|x|^2$ under the system of constraints $Ax=b$, we introduce a vector $\lambda$ of Lagrange multipliers and consider the function $f(x)=x^*x-(Ax-b)^*\lambda$. Its gradient is $2x-A^*\lambda$, and setting this to zero yields $\hat x=A^*\lambda/2$. Thus $\hat x$ is in the column space of $A^*$. 
 Now there can be only one solution of $Ax-b$ in the orthogonal complement of the null space of $A$. If $x_1$ and $x_2$ are two solutions, then $A(x_1-x_2)=Ax_1-Ax_2=(Ax_1-b)-(Ax_2-b)=0$, so their difference is in the null space of $A$. If the solutions are both in the orthogonal complement of the null space, then so is their difference; since the difference is both in the null space and in its orthogonal complement, it must be zero. 
 Thus it suffices to show that $A^+b$ solves $Ax-b$ and lies in the column space of $A^*$. We know that if $Ax-b$ has solutions then $A^+b$ is one of them, because $A^+b$ minimizes the error norm. We also know that $A^+b$ lies in the column space of $A^*$, since    $A^+b=(A^*A^{+*}A^+)b=A^*(A^{+*}A^+b)$  .

Mt_a: To map the slider's current value to a percentage between the minimum and maximum, subtract the minimum value (174) from the current value (n) to get the offset from the minimum. Given a series, how does one calculate that limit below? I noticed the numerator is an arithmetic progression and the denominator is a geometric progression — if that's of any relevance —, but I still don't know how to solve it. 
 $$\lim_{n\to\infty} \sum^n_{k=0} \frac{k+1}{3^k}$$ 
 I did it "by hand" and the result should be $\frac{9}{4}.$
Rq_a: How can we evaluate the infinite sum $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{k+1}{3^k}$$, where the numerator forms an arithmetic progression and the denominator a geometric progression? Is there a probabilistic or expectation-based approach that can simplify the calculation?
Mt_a:
1. Recognize that the terms resemble the expectation of a function of a geometric random variable.
2. Define a geometric random variable $X$ with probability of success $p=2/3$, so that $P(X=k) = (1-p)^{k-1}p = \frac{2}{3^k}$ for $k=1,2,3,...$.
3. Recall that the expected value $E(X) = 1/p$ for a geometric distribution.
4. Note that $E(X+1) = E(X) + 1 = \frac{3}{2} + 1 = \frac{5}{2}$.
5. Observe that $E(X+1) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (k+1)P(X=k) = 2 \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{k+1}{3^k}$.
6. Solve for $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{k+1}{3^k}$ by dividing both sides by 2, yielding $\frac{5}{4}$.
7. Recognize that the original sum starts at $k=0$, so add the $k=0$ term: $\frac{0+1}{3^0} = 1$.
8. Therefore, the total sum is $1 + \frac{5}{4} = \frac{9}{4}$.
Ra_a: By relating the sum to the expectation of a geometric random variable and adjusting for the starting index, the value of the infinite sum is $\boxed{\frac{9}{4}}$.
Rq_b: How can we explicitly compute the infinite sum $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{k+1}{3^k}$$ by manipulating and regrouping its terms, possibly using properties of geometric series?
Mt_b:
1. Expand the sum to observe its structure: $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{k+1}{3^k} = 1 + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{3}{9} + \frac{4}{27} + \dots$.
2. Notice that each term $\frac{k+1}{3^k}$ can be interpreted as adding $k+1$ copies of $1/3^k$.
3. Rearrange the sum by grouping all terms that share the same denominator, forming nested geometric series.
4. Express the sum as a series of geometric series with decreasing starting points: $\left(1 + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{9} + \dots\right) + \left(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{9} + \dots\right) + \left(\frac{1}{9} + \dots\right) + \dots$.
5. Recognize that each group is a geometric series with sum $S = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{3^n} = \frac{3}{2}$.
6. Sum these groups, noting that each subsequent group omits the first term of the previous group.
7. Use the formula for the partial sum $S_k = \frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^k$ to express the sum in terms of $S$.
8. Combine the results to find $\frac{3}{2} + \frac{1}{2}S = \frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{4} = \frac{9}{4}$.
Ra_b: By regrouping terms and applying the formula for geometric series, the sum converges to $\boxed{\frac{9}{4}}$.

Let $X$ be a geometric random variable with probability of success $p=2/3$, so that
$$
{\rm P}(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p = \frac{2}{{3^k }}, \;\; k=1,2,3,\ldots.
$$
From the easy-to-remember fact that ${\rm E}(X)=1/p$, it follows that
$$
\frac{3}{2} + 1 = {\rm E}(X) + 1 = {\rm E}(X + 1) = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^\infty  {(k + 1){\rm P}(X = k) = 2\sum\limits_{k = 1}^\infty  {\frac{{k + 1}}{{3^k }}} } .
$$
Hence
$$
\sum\limits_{k = 1}^\infty  {\frac{{k + 1}}{{3^k }}} = \frac{5}{4}.
$$

Rq_a: How can any number less than n! be uniquely represented in the factorial number system (factoradic), and what is the reasoning behind this decomposition? Please explain the process and its uniqueness.
Mt_a: The factorial number system, or factoradic, allows us to represent any integer less than n! as a sum of multiples of factorials with specific coefficients. To construct this representation, consider the permutation orderings of n elements. For each position in the permutation, you select an element from the remaining set, and the choices correspond to the coefficients in the factoradic representation. The process is: for the first position, there are n choices, so the coefficient is a_{n-1}; for the second, n-1 choices, so a_{n-2}; and so on, until the last position, which has only one choice (a_0 = 0). This method is also known as the Lehmer code. The uniqueness comes from the fact that each integer less than n! corresponds to exactly one permutation, and thus one unique sequence of coefficients.
Ra_a: Yes, every number less than n! can be uniquely represented in the factorial number system (factoradic), using a process that corresponds to the ordering of permutations (Lehmer code).
Rq_b: Why is the representation of a number in the factorial number system unique, and how does the process of finding this representation compare to finding a number's representation in a standard base (such as base 3)? Please describe the algorithm for constructing the factorial representation.
Mt_b: The uniqueness of the factorial number system representation is analogous to how numbers are represented in other bases. In base 3, for example, you repeatedly take the remainder when dividing by 3 to get each digit, then divide by 3 and repeat. For the factorial number system, you start with i = 2, and for each step, the next digit is n mod i. Then you divide n by i (integer division), increment i by 1, and repeat the process until n becomes zero. This stepwise process ensures that each number less than n! has a unique sequence of digits (coefficients) corresponding to the factorials, just as in standard positional bases.
Ra_b: The factorial number system representation is unique, and you can find it by repeatedly taking n mod i (starting with i = 2), dividing n by i, and incrementing i, similar to finding digits in other bases.

This is some permutation $(s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n)$. Now for $s_1$ you had $n$ choices (label them $0$ to $n-1$) and you picked one, so let $a_{n-1}$ be the choice you made. For $s_2$ you had $n-1$ choices (label them $0$ to $n-2$) and you picked one, so let $a_{n-2}$ be the number of the choice you made. It is the end of the day and my brain just can't cope anymore. Can anyone help with, what I hope, is a simple question?  
 Given a point on a circle ($x$, $y$ coordinates) how can I calculate the coordinates of another point at a given distance around the circumference of the circle? Known variables are the starting point, distance traveled and radius of the circle.
Rq_a: Given a circle with center at $(a, b)$ and radius $r$, and a starting point $(x, y)$ on the circumference, how can we compute the coordinates of a new point that lies a distance $D$ along the circumference from the starting point (in either the clockwise or counterclockwise direction)? Please provide a detailed mathematical derivation, including any necessary transformations and formulas.
Mt_a:
1. Translate the circle so its center $(a, b)$ is at the origin, moving the starting point to $(u, v) = (x-a, y-b)$.
2. Determine the initial angle $\theta$ between the positive $x$-axis and the vector $(u, v)$, using $\cos\theta = u/r$ and $\sin\theta = v/r$.
3. Calculate the angle $\phi = D/r$ corresponding to the arc length $D$ (positive for counterclockwise, negative for clockwise travel).
4. The new angle after traveling is $\theta + \phi$.
5. The new coordinates in the translated system are $(r\cos(\theta+\phi), r\sin(\theta+\phi))$.
6. Translate back to the original center by adding $(a, b)$, yielding $(a + r\cos(\theta+\phi), b + r\sin(\theta+\phi))$.
7. Alternatively, use the rotation formula to directly compute the new coordinates: $(a + (x-a)\cos\phi - (y-b)\sin\phi, b + (x-a)\sin\phi + (y-b)\cos\phi)$, where $\phi = D/r$.
Ra_a:
To find the coordinates of the new point after traveling a distance $D$ along the circle from $(x, y)$, use:
$$(a + (x-a)\cos\phi - (y-b)\sin\phi,\; b + (x-a)\sin\phi + (y-b)\cos\phi),$$
where $\phi = D/r$ and $(a, b)$ is the center of the circle.
Rq_b: Suppose you have a circle centered at $c = a + b i$ in the complex plane, and a starting point $z_0 = x_0 + i y_0$ on the circumference. How can you use complex numbers and Euler's formula to determine the coordinates of a point that is a distance $d$ along the circumference from $z_0$ (counterclockwise), given the radius $r$? Please provide the derivation and the final Cartesian coordinate formulas.
Mt_b:
1. Represent the center as $c = a + b i$ and the starting point as $z_0 = x_0 + i y_0$.
2. Express $z_0$ in terms of the center and radius: $z_0 = c + r e^{i\phi}$, where $\phi$ is the initial angle.
3. The angle corresponding to distance $d$ along the circumference is $\theta = d/r$.
4. The new point after traveling is $z_1 = c + r e^{i(\phi + \theta)}$.
5. Alternatively, $z_1 = c + (z_0 - c) e^{i\theta}$.
6. Expand $e^{i\theta}$ using Euler's formula to convert back to Cartesian coordinates.
7. The resulting coordinates are:
   $x_1 = a + (x_0 - a) \cos(d/r) - (y_0 - b) \sin(d/r)$
   $y_1 = b + (x_0 - a) \sin(d/r) + (y_0 - b) \cos(d/r)$
Ra_b:
The coordinates of the new point are:
$$
  x_1 = a + (x_0 - a) \cos(d/r) - (y_0 - b) \sin(d/r)
$$
$$
  y_1 = b + (x_0 - a) \sin(d/r) + (y_0 - b) \cos(d/r)
$$
where $(a, b)$ is the center, $(x_0, y_0)$ is the starting point, $r$ is the radius, and $d$ is the distance traveled along the circle.

Let the center of the circle be $(a,b)$.   Drag  the center to the origin. This procedure drags our given point $(x,y)$ to $(x-a,y-b)$. 
 For simplicity of notation, let $u=x-a$, $v=y-b$.  Now we determine the angle that the positive $x$-axis has to be rotated through (counterclockwise) to hit the line from the origin to $(u,v)$.  Call this angle $\theta$. 
 Then $\theta$ is the angle, say in the interval $(-\pi,\pi]$, whose cosine is $u/r$, and whose sine is $v/r$, where $r$ is the radius of the circle.  (This was already known; it also happens to be $\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$.)  So from now on we can take $\theta$ as known.  But we have to be careful to take the signs of $u$ and $v$ into account when calculating $\theta$.  
 Let $D$ be the distance travelled. Assume that we are travelling counterclockwise. Then the angle of travel is (in radians) equal to $D/r$. Let $\phi$ be this angle. If we are travelling clockwise, just replace $\phi$ by $-\phi$.  So from now on we can take $\phi$ as known.   
 After the travel, our angle is $\theta+\phi$.  This means that we are at the point with coordinates 
 $$(r\cos(\theta+\phi), \: \: r\sin(\theta+\phi)).$$ 
 Now transform back, by adding $(a,b)$ to the point.  We obtain
$$(a+r\cos(\theta+\phi),\:\: b+r\sin(\theta+\phi)).$$ 
 All the components of this formula are known, so we can compute the answer. 
 Comment :  Note that 
$$\cos(\theta+\phi)=\cos\theta\cos\phi-\sin\theta\sin\phi.$$
But we know that $r\cos\theta=u$ and $r\sin\theta=v$.
Thus 
$$a+r\cos(\theta+\phi)=a+u\cos\phi-v\sin\phi.$$ 
 Similarly, 
$$\sin(\theta+\phi)=\cos\theta\sin\phi+\sin\theta\cos\phi,$$
and therefore
$$b+r\sin(\theta+\phi)=u\sin\phi+v\cos\phi.$$
Thus an alternate (and for many purposes simpler) version of the answer is
$$(a+(x-a)\cos\phi-(y-b)\sin\phi,\:\: b+(x-a)\sin\phi+(y-b)\cos\phi),$$
where $\phi=D/r$.  
 We could also reach this by quoting the rotation formula. Recall that when we are rotating a point $(u,v)$ about the origin through an angle $\phi$, we multiply the vector by a certain matrix.  You can think of this post as being, in particular, a derivation of the rotation formula.

2. Compute the direction vector I am facing by combining the north and east vectors at my position, weighted by the cosine and sine of my facing direction.
3. Calculate the vector from my position to the object's position.
4. Use the dot product between my facing direction vector and the vector to the object to determine if the object is in front of me (positive dot product).
5. Calculate the angle between my facing direction and the object using the dot product formula for vectors.
6. If this angle is less than half the viewport (i.e., 90° for a 180° viewport), and the surface distance between my position and the object's position is less than or equal to 1 km, then the object is within my viewport.

Specifically, is there a practical method for representing and updating a Bezier curve such that users can drag special points on the curve itself, and the underlying control points are recalculated accordingly to maintain the curve passing through these points? What are the standard parameter values or approaches for such a system, and how can this be implemented for cubic curves?
Mt_a:
1. Direct manipulation of arbitrary points on a Bezier curve is mathematically complex, especially for cubic curves.
2. A practical solution is to define a set of 'special' points on the curve at fixed parameter values (e.g., t=0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 for cubic Beziers).
3. Users can move these special points, and the system periodically recalculates the Bezier control points so that the curve passes through the updated positions of these points.
4. The conversion from the four points on the curve (U0, U1, U2, U3) to Bezier control points (P0, P1, P2, P3) can be done using established formulas, such as John Burkardt's method.
5. The resulting Bezier curve will interpolate the endpoints and the two intermediate points, and can be rendered using standard Bezier plotting routines.
6. While other parameter values can be used, t=0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 is common and effective.

Rq_b: What is an algorithmic method for enabling users to 'grab' and move a point directly on a Bezier curve (such as a cubic or quadratic), and have the nearest control point update so that the curve passes through the new location at the same parameter value? 2. Determine which control point is 'nearest' in parametric space to the selected point. For cubic curves, this can be based on dividing the parameter range into segments.
3. Compute the change in position (ΔPt) for the selected point on the curve.
4. Calculate the basis (weighting) function value for the chosen control point at parameter t.
5. Update the chosen control point's position by adding ΔPt divided by the basis function value at t.
6. This process can be generalized for any basis function (Bezier, B-spline, etc.), and works for both quadratic and cubic curves.
Ra_b: To let users move a point on a Bezier curve and update the curve accordingly, find the parameter value (t) of the selected point, identify the nearest control point, and move that control point by the change in position divided by its basis function value at t. Here is my rewrite followed by the original I found on the net. 
 If the formatting is too screwy, email me for an original on my site or...
noskosteve /at/ Yahoo /dot/ com: 
 PAGE 1 
 How to "grab" a spot on a curve to move it (familiar notation). 
 For a parmetric cubic curve, a point on the curve at parameter t (Pt) is defined by: 
 P(t) or Pt  = Sum Pi*Bi(t)   =   P1B1(t)  +  P2B2(t)  +  P3B3(t)  + P4B4(t). 
 Pi are the 4 control points and Bi are the respective weighting functions. 
 To "grab" a spot on the curve and relocate it, you are moving some Pt to Pt'.  Let the amount you move it be Pt = (New point - old point)  =  Pt'- Pt. 
 Choose a control point to be moved. (see page 2).  Any will do, but choosing the "closest" in parametric space works best.  Let's say we'll move P2. Call the new position P2'. 
 This makes P2 = P2' - P2 
 The old point on the curve was:      Pt = P1B1(t) + P2B2(t) + P3B3(t) + P4B4(t) 
 The new point on the curve will be:  Pt'= P1B1(t) + P2'B2(t) + P3B3(t) + P4B4(t) 
 Subtract the Old from the New:    Pt = Pt'- Pt  =  (P2' - P2) B2(t) = P2*B2(t) 
 Solving for P2:      P2 = Pt / B2(t) 
 Then solve for the New P2 (P2'):   P2' = P2 + [ Pt / B2(t) ] 
 OR    P2' =  P2 + (  [Pt'- Pt] /  B2(t)   ) 
 So... In general:
Given: a point on the curve called Pt at parameter "t", "near" control point "n".
To move that point on the curve to a new location which differs in position by Pt, move Pn by Pt/Bn(t) 
 In other words:
    Select a spot on the curve to be moved and its new location.
    Determine the parameter value of this spot.
    Calculate the change in spot position, Pt.
    Divide this change, Pt, by the basis function (for the target control point or Bn(t) ) which is evaluated at the selected parameter (t). 
    Finally, add this to the control point (P2) location.  This is the same function and t for all dimensions, so only one calculation is required. 
 Note that this requires calculating the weighting function for the target control point at the parameter value (t) of the location selected on the curve.  You obtain it from the scan for the target "t". 
 This works with any basis function. 
 Concept: 
 
 if Curve = Control Pt*Weight 
       then Control Pt = Curve / Weight    
 
 PAGE 2 
 Further areas for consideration. 
 Finding the point on the curve to be moved. 
 First, the parameter value of the selected (grabbed) location on the curve must be determined.  This must be a sequential search rather than binary because the curve may double back.  This could make the true closest point "un-findable" if the curve approaches then moves away from the cursor before going back to closest location the cursor.  It can be a coarse-fine search, such as stepping in t steps of 0.1 or larger to find the bracketing locations, then subdividing that sub-segment to hit the curve.  The limit being the closest to the nearest pixel on the screen. 
 This takes the form of re-calculating the curve without needing to draw it; only calculating the distance. 
 Choosing the target control point.

query: As you know, in RSA encryption, we calculate an n value by multiplying two long primes. Then we calculate Φ(n), which is equal to (p-1)(q-1). After that, we choose an encryption key which satisfies gcd(e,Φ(n))=1. I know that it is necessary to calculate decryption key, which is the modular inverse of e. My question is: Why do we use Φ(n) in determination of encryption and decryption key processes? How can one prove it is working for RSA encryption?

Please provide a detailed explanation and proof.
Mt_a:
1. In RSA, the modulus n is the product of two primes, p and q. The set of integers relatively prime to n forms a multiplicative group modulo n, whose order is Φ(n).
2. Euler's theorem states that for any integer M coprime to n, M^{Φ(n)} ≡ 1 mod n.
3. Encryption is performed by computing C = M^e mod n, and decryption by computing M = C^d mod n.
4. To ensure decryption recovers the original message, we require that ed ≡ 1 mod Φ(n), so that ed = rΦ(n) + 1 for some integer r.
5. Then, M^{ed} = M^{rΦ(n)+1} = (M^{Φ(n)})^r * M ≡ 1^r * M ≡ M mod n, thus recovering the original message.
6. Therefore, Φ(n) is used because it is the order of the group, and its properties guarantee that the modular inverse relationship between e and d enables correct decryption.
Ra_a: We use Φ(n) because it is the order of the multiplicative group modulo n, and Euler's theorem ensures that choosing e and d such that ed ≡ 1 mod Φ(n) allows the encryption and decryption processes to correctly recover the original message in RSA.
Rq_b: What is the mathematical reason for using Euler's totient function Φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1) in the selection of encryption and decryption keys in RSA, and how does this choice guarantee that the encryption function is invertible and decryption is unique? Please provide a proof.
Mt_b:
1. In RSA, Φ(n) is the order of the group of invertible integers modulo n.
2. The encryption exponent e is chosen such that gcd(e, Φ(n)) = 1, ensuring that the mapping x → x^e mod n is one-to-one (invertible).
3. If x^e ≡ y^e mod n, then (x/y)^e ≡ 1 mod n. By Euler's theorem, (x/y)^{Φ(n)} ≡ 1 mod n.
4. By group theory, if gcd(e, Φ(n)) = 1, the only solution to z^e ≡ 1 mod n is z ≡ 1 mod n, so x ≡ y mod n.
5. Therefore, the encryption function is invertible, and the decryption exponent d (the modular inverse of e modulo Φ(n)) exists and is unique, ensuring unique decryption.
Ra_b: Φ(n) is used because it is the order of the invertible group modulo n, and choosing e coprime to Φ(n) guarantees that encryption is invertible and decryption is unique in RSA.

Short answer.  We use $\Phi(n)$ because that is the order of the multiplicative group of units modulo $n=pq$. 
 Long answer.  RSA works via modular exponentiation modulo $n$. The idea is to take a message that corresponds to a number $M$, "encrypt" it by raising it some power $e$ to obtain an encyphered text $M^e$; and then "decrypt" by raising it to an appropriate power $d$ to recover $M$. The reason this works is that the multiplicative group of units modulo $n$ is a  finite  group, and by Euler's Theorem we know that $M^{\Phi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod{n}$ for all $M$ that is relatively prime to $n$.  
 That means that for every integer $k$ we have
$$M^{\Phi(n)+k} = M^{\Phi(n)}M^k \equiv 1\cdot M^k =M^k\pmod{n}.$$ 
 That is, raising a number that is realtively prime to $n$ to the $\Phi(n)$-th power will "kill it": make it congruent to $1$.  
 In order to be able to recover $M$ from $M^e$ by exponentiation, we need there to exist a $d$ such that $M\equiv (M^e)^d = M^{ed}\pmod{n}$. But for this to be possible, we want $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\Phi(n)}$; because if $ed\equiv 1 \pmod{\Phi(n)}$, then we can write $ed = r\Phi(n) + 1$ for some $r$, and then
$$M^{ed} = M^{r\Phi(n)+1} = (M^{\Phi(n)})^rM \equiv 1^r\cdot M = M \pmod{n},$$
and we have recovered $M$.

I have a set of solutions to an equation, which are all very similar to spherical harmonics. The solutions are discretised on a regular 3d grid. I would like to label them with which spherical harmonic they are most like, so the $l$ and $m$ values for each one. 
 Theoretically this is just selecting the largest coefficient from a decomposition of each solution vector onto the spherical harmonic space, or a transform of some kind. 
 Is there a cheap/simple way to calculate which harmonic each solution is nearest?
Rq_a: Given a set of functions defined on a regular 3D grid that closely resemble spherical harmonics, how can I efficiently determine, for each function, the spherical harmonic (specified by quantum numbers $l$ and $m$) to which it is most similar? Specifically, is there a straightforward computational method to project each discretized solution onto the spherical harmonic basis and identify the dominant component, ideally using a least-squares approach or similar transform?
Mt_a:
1. Represent each function on the grid as a linear combination of spherical harmonics, with unknown coefficients $c_{lm}$. 
2. Set up a least-squares minimization problem to fit the function values on the grid to this linear combination, minimizing the squared difference between the original function and its spherical harmonic expansion. 
3. This leads to a system of linear equations for the coefficients $c_{lm}$, which can be solved using standard linear algebra techniques. 
4. If the grid points are within a spherical volume, the sums over the grid can approximate integrals, and due to the orthogonality of spherical harmonics, the system simplifies: the matrix becomes nearly diagonal, and the coefficients $c_{lm}$ can be computed directly as sums over the grid. 
5. The spherical harmonic with the largest coefficient magnitude indicates which harmonic the function is closest to.
Ra_a: You can efficiently determine the closest spherical harmonic for each solution by performing a linear least-squares fit of your discretized function to the spherical harmonic basis, then identifying the $l$ and $m$ corresponding to the largest coefficient in this expansion. If your grid is approximately spherical, the computation simplifies further, as the orthogonality of the harmonics allows you to directly compute the coefficients as sums over the grid points.
Rq_b: Assuming my discretized functions on a 3D grid are nearly independent of the radial coordinate and closely resemble a single spherical harmonic, is there a computationally efficient way to estimate which spherical harmonic (i.e., which $l$ and $m$) each function is closest to, possibly by using properties of the Laplacian or gradient on the sphere to narrow down the search before computing coefficients?
Mt_b:
1. Assume each function is primarily a function of the angular variables $(\theta, \phi)$ and is well approximated by a single spherical harmonic. 
2. Recognize that the dominant $l$ value can be estimated by considering the ratio of the function's gradient squared integral to its squared integral over the sphere, as the Laplacian eigenvalues of spherical harmonics are proportional to $l(l+1)$. 
3. Compute $\tilde{l} = \lfloor \sqrt{\int |\nabla f|^2 / \int f^2} \rfloor$ to estimate the likely $l$ value. 
4. Restrict the search for the dominant spherical harmonic to a small range around $\tilde{l}$ (e.g., $[\tilde{l}-2, \tilde{l}+2]$), and for each $l$ in this range, compute the coefficients for all admissible $m$. 
5. The pair $(l, m)$ with the largest coefficient identifies the closest spherical harmonic.
Ra_b: You can estimate the dominant $l$ value by computing the ratio of the squared gradient integral to the squared function integral, then restrict your spherical harmonic decomposition to a small range of $l$ values around this estimate. By computing the coefficients only for this subset, you can efficiently identify the $l$ and $m$ corresponding to the closest spherical harmonic for each function.
output_a:
You could do a standard  linear least-squares fit  to a linear combination of spherical harmonics with variable coefficients: 
 $$f(\vec x)=\sum_{lm}c_{lm}Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi)$$ 
 $$\sum_{\vec x}\left|f(\vec x)-f_{\vec x}\right|^2\rightarrow \min$$ 
 $$\sum_{\vec x}\left|\sum_{lm}c_{lm}Y_{lm}(\theta,\phi)-f_{\vec x}\right|^2\rightarrow \min$$ 
 $$\sum_{\vec x}Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)\left(\sum_{l'm'}c_{l'm'}Y_{l'm'}(\theta,\phi)-f_{\vec x}\right)=0$$ 
 $$\sum_{l'm'}\left(\sum_{\vec x}Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)Y_{l'm'}(\theta,\phi)\right)c_{lm}=\sum_{\vec x}Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)f_{\vec x}\;,$$ 
 where $\theta$ and $\phi$ are the angular variables corresponding to $\vec x$, $f(\vec x)$ is the fitted function and $f_{\vec x}$ are the function values you have on the grid. This is a system of linear equations for the coefficients $c_{lm}$; you could solve it and say that your function is "nearest" to the spherical harmonic whose coefficient has the highest magnitude. 
 However, by using only function values within a spherical volume, you can consider the inner sum on the left-hand side as an approximation of an integral: 
 $$
\begin{eqnarray}
\sum_{\vec x}Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)Y_{l'm'}(\theta,\phi)
&\approx&
\int Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)Y_{l'm'}(\theta,\phi)\mathrm dV
\\
&=&
\iint Y^*_{lm}(\theta,\phi)Y_{l'm'}(\theta,\phi)\mathrm d\Omega r^2\mathrm dr
\\
&=&
\delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}\int r^2\mathrm dr
\\
&=&
\frac13\delta_{ll'}\delta_{mm'}R^3\;,
\end{eqnarray}
$$ 
 where $R$ is the radius of the spherical volume. This may actually be quite a good approximation if you have e.g. a cubical grid, since the symmetry of the grid causes many of the coefficients approximated as zero to actually vanish. 
 This radically simplifies the least-squares solution, since the matrix on the left is now the identity and the coefficients are simply given by the sums on the right.

I'm trying to calculate the 2D fourier transform of this function: 
 $$\frac{1}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}$$ 
 I only want to do the fourier transform for x and y (and leave z as it is). 
 So far, I've tried using the method of residues (assuming $k_x$ > 0 and closing the contour on the top), but I'm left with $$\frac{e^{ik_x x}}{[(x - ic)(x+ic)]^{3/2}}$$ 
 (where c depends only on y and z). And because of the fractional power on the bottom I'm not sure how to get the residue. I've also tried using polar coordinates but that didn't get me anywhere. Does anyone know how I should proceed? 
 Also, I know the answer should look like $e^{- \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2}z}$.
Rq_a: How can I explicitly compute the two-dimensional Fourier transform (with respect to x and y) of the function $f(x, y, z) = \frac{1}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$, leaving z as a parameter, and what are the detailed steps, especially if using polar coordinates and Bessel functions?
Mt_a:
1. Change variables to polar coordinates: set $x = r \cos \varphi$ and $y = r \sin \varphi$.
2. The Fourier transform becomes an integral over $r$ and $\varphi$:
   $$
   \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^2} \int_0^{2\pi} d\varphi \int_0^{\infty} r dr \, e^{i k_x r \cos \varphi + i k_y r \sin \varphi} (r^2 + z^2)^{-3/2}
   $$
3. Combine the exponents: $k_x \cos \varphi + k_y \sin \varphi = \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2} \cos(\varphi + \varphi_0)$.
4. The $\varphi$ integral yields a Bessel function: $J_0(r \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2})$.
5. The integral reduces to:
   $$
   \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{\infty} dr \, \frac{r}{(r^2 + z^2)^{3/2}} J_0(r \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2})
   $$
6. This $r$-integral can be evaluated using Mellin transform or convolution techniques, resulting in:
   $$
   \frac{1}{2 \pi |z|} e^{- |z| \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2}}
   $$
Ra_a: The two-dimensional Fourier transform of $\frac{1}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$ with respect to $x$ and $y$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi |z|} e^{- |z| \sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2}}$.
Rq_b: Is there a way to compute the 2D Fourier transform of $\frac{1}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$ by interpreting it as a fundamental solution to a higher-dimensional Laplace equation, and how does this approach lead to the answer without explicit integration?
Mt_b:
1. Recognize that $\frac{1}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}$ is (up to a constant) the fundamental solution to the 5-dimensional Laplace equation.
2. Denote $\Gamma(x, y, z_1, z_2, z_3) = \frac{1}{3 \sigma_5 (x^2 + y^2 + |z|^2)^{3/2}}$, where $\sigma_5$ is the volume of the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^5$.
3. The Laplacian $\Delta \Gamma = \delta(x, y, z_1, z_2, z_3)$.
4. The original function is $f(x, y, |z|) = 3 \sigma_5 \Gamma(x, y, z_1, z_2, z_3)$.
5. Taking the Fourier transform in $x$ and $y$ of the Laplace equation gives:
   $$
   \Delta \tilde{\Gamma}(z_1, z_2, z_3) - k^2 \tilde{\Gamma}(z_1, z_2, z_3) = \delta(z_1, z_2, z_3)
   $$
   where $k^2 = k_x^2 + k_y^2$.
6. This is the equation for the fundamental solution of the 3D Helmholtz equation with negative sign, whose solution is $\frac{e^{-k|z|}}{4\pi |z|}$ (the decaying solution at infinity).
7. Therefore, the Fourier transform is $\frac{e^{-k|z|}}{4\pi |z|}$, matching the expected form.
Ra_b: By interpreting the function as a fundamental solution to the 5D Laplace equation and applying the Fourier transform in $x$ and $y$, the result is $\frac{e^{-\sqrt{k_x^2 + k_y^2} |z|}}{4\pi |z|}$.

I'm beginning to study probability and an exercise in the study guide that asks me to calculate: What is the probability that the month January, of one year randomly selected have only four Sundays? 
 the solution of the book indicates that it's 4 / 7 which is equal to 0.5714 probability that the event occurs, according to what I learned in class the probability of this event can be calculated by counting probability as it is possible to have all elements of the sample space, and all the elements that belong to threw the probability of which is to be calculated. 
 P (A) = number of cases occurring A / number of cases in the sample space
 
 My question is why the sample space of this experiment is 7 and what is the maximum number of Sundays in January that may have (I think by intuition that can be 5) 
 This formula applies when it is possible to have all elements of the sample space, and all items pertaining to the event whose probability is to be calculated
Rq_a: Why is the sample space for determining the probability that January in a randomly selected year has only four Sundays considered to have 7 elements, and how does the starting day of January affect the number of Sundays in the month? Additionally, what is the maximum number of Sundays that January can have?
Mt_a: First, consider that January can start on any day of the week, so there are 7 possible starting days. If January starts on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, there are only 4 Sundays in the month; if it starts on Thursday, Friday, Saturday, or Sunday, there are 5 Sundays. Assuming each starting day is equally likely, the probability of having 4 Sundays is the number of favorable starting days (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday) divided by the total number of possible starting days (7), giving 4/7. The maximum number of Sundays in January is 5. However, in the Gregorian calendar, the distribution of starting days is not perfectly even over long cycles, but for most practical purposes, the sample space is taken as 7.
Ra_a: The sample space is 7 because January can start on any day of the week, and the number of Sundays depends on the starting day. The maximum number of Sundays in January is 5.
Rq_b: How is the probability calculated that January in a randomly chosen year has exactly four Sundays, considering the possible starting days of the month and the structure of the Gregorian calendar? Also, what is the maximum number of Sundays that January can have?
Mt_b: There are 7 possible days on which January 1st can fall, and each is nearly equally likely. If January 1st is a Sunday, Friday, or Saturday, January will have 5 Sundays; if it is a Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday, there will be 4 Sundays. Thus, in 4 out of 7 cases, January has 4 Sundays, so the probability is 4/7. However, due to the Gregorian calendar's 400-year cycle, the distribution is not perfectly even: over 400 years, the first of January falls 56 times on Monday and Saturday, 57 times on Wednesday and Thursday, and 58 times on Sunday, Tuesday, and Friday. The exact probability is therefore (56+58+57+57)/400 = 228/400 = 0.57. The maximum number of Sundays in January is 5.
Ra_b: The probability that January has exactly four Sundays is approximately 4/7, but the exact value is 228/400 = 0.57 due to the Gregorian calendar's structure. The maximum number of Sundays in January is 5.

The idea is that January can start on any day of the week.  If it starts Thursday through Sunday, there are 5 Sundays, while if it starts Monday through Wednesday, there are only 4.  So if starting days are evenly distributed, the probability would be 4/7.  The maximum number doesn't figure in.  The sample space is the starting day of the week. 
 This answer is close, but not right.  In the Gregorian calendar the days repeat in a 400 year cycle as 400*365+97=146097 is divisible by 7.  If you look carefully, the start days of January are not (quite) evenly distributed.
output_b:
The year can begin on any one of the seven days of the week, and each of the seven is equally likely. (Actually, this isn’t quite true, but you have to look very closely at the Gregorian calendar to see that it isn’t, and the deviation from equal likelihood is very small indeed.)  Thus, the probability that 1 January falls on a Sunday is $1/7$, the probability that it falls on a Monday is $1/7$, and so on. Suppose that 1 January falls on a Sunday.  Then the Sundays in January fall on 1 January, 8 January, 15 January, 22 January, and 29 January, so there are five of them. What happens if 1 January is a Saturday? Then the Sundays fall on 2, 9, 16, 23, and 30 January, and there are again five of them. Similarly, if 1 January falls on a Friday, the Sundays fall on 3, 10, 17, 24, and 31 January, and once more there are five of them. I’ll leave you to check for yourself, using the same kind of analysis, that if 1 January falls on a Thursday, Wednesday, Tuesday, or Monday, there are just four Sundays in the month. Thus, in four of the seven equally likely cases January has four Sundays, and the probability of its having four Sundays is therefore $4/7$. (And as you can see, the maximum possible number of Sundays in January is indeed five.) 
 Added:  If I’ve not miscounted, in the course of the $400$-year Gregorian cycle the first of the year falls $56$ times each on Monday and Saturday, $57$ times each on Wednesday and Thursday, and $58$ times each on Sunday, Tuesday, and Friday. The exact probability of getting just four Sundays in January is therefore $\frac{56+58+57+57}{400} = \frac{228}{400} = 0.57$, slightly less than $4/7$.

Rq_a: Given a truly fair and random two-sided device (such as a magical coin), where each flip is independent of the previous ones, and knowing that sequences like 8 heads in a row will inevitably occur in an unlimited number of flips, does the occurrence of 8 consecutive heads affect the probability of the next flip being heads? Mt_a:
1. Each flip of a fair, independent coin has a probability of 1/2 for heads and 1/2 for tails, regardless of previous outcomes.
2. The occurrence of 8 heads in a row is a rare but expected event over many trials, but it does not influence the probability of the next flip.
3. If the coin is truly fair and independent, the best estimate for the next flip remains 1/2 for heads.
4. If you observe 8 heads in a row, you might question the fairness of the coin, but if fairness is guaranteed, your belief should not change.

Ra_a: If the coin is truly fair and flips are independent, the probability of the next toss being heads is still 1/2, even after 8 heads in a row. You should bet on either side, as both are equally likely.

2. Both of these beliefs are incorrect if the coin is truly fair and flips are independent; the probability remains 1/2 for either outcome.
3. To illustrate, imagine a scenario where many coins are flipped repeatedly, and only those that land heads are kept and flipped again. Eventually, you may find a coin that has landed heads many times in a row, but this does not make it any more or less likely to land heads or tails on the next flip.
4. The idea that a coin is 'overdue' for tails or is on a 'hot streak' is a fallacy; each flip is independent and unaffected by previous results.
Ra_b: Even after 8 heads in a row, the probability of the next flip being heads or tails is still 1/2; beliefs about being 'overdue' or 'on a streak' are incorrect for a fair, independent coin.

query:
How do you calculate this limit
$$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to 0} \frac{{\sin (\sin x)}}{x}?$$
without derivatives please.
Thanks.
Rq_a: How can we evaluate the limit $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{x}$$ without using derivatives, perhaps by manipulating the expression or using known trigonometric limits?
Mt_a: First, rewrite the original limit as the product $$\frac{\sin(\sin x)}{x} = \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{\sin x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{x}.$$ Next, recall the standard limit $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.$$ As $x \to 0$, $\sin x \to 0$, so we can also use the substitution $y = \sin x$ to see that $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{\sin x} = \lim_{y \to 0} \frac{\sin y}{y} = 1.$$ Therefore, the original limit is the product $1 \cdot 1 = 1.$
Ra_a: The limit is 1.
Rq_b: How can we compute $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{x}$$ without derivatives, perhaps by using geometric proofs or known trigonometric limits?
Mt_b: First, recall the geometric proof that $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1.$$ Also, as $x \to 0$, $\sin x \to 0$. Using these facts, we can write $$\frac{\sin(\sin x)}{x} = \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{\sin x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{x}.$$ Both factors approach 1 as $x \to 0$, so their product is 1.
Ra_b: The limit equals 1.
output_a:
Write the limit as
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{\sin x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{x}.$$
It is well-known that
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1,$$
and since $\sin x \to 0$ as $x \to 0$, we get that also
$$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(\sin x)}{\sin x} = 1.$$
Therefore the limit is $1 \cdot 1 = 1$.

query:
I have a rotation over time represented as a series of Euler angles (heading, pitch and bank).  I'd like to represent the individual rotation curves as continuously as possible.  An anyone help me with how I would calculate the equivalent Euler angle representations for a single rotation, from where I could derive the "closest" equivalent to the prior rotation in time? 
 Thanks! 
 
 I realize that half the problem may be my inability to properly express the problem in the first place.  Perhaps a concrete example might make it a bit clearer.  I have two rotations around a common $xyz$ axis expressed in degrees as Euler angles: $(-224.782, 265, 214.25)$ and $(-44.782, -85, 34.215)$.  These produce an equivalent orientation.  Supposing that I started with the latter, which is "normalized" to the range to $-180 \leq x \leq 180$, $-90\leq y\leq 90$, $-180 \leq z \leq 180$, how would I arrive at the former? Apologies for the layman explanation.
Rq_a: How can I represent a time-varying rotation, originally given as a sequence of Euler angles (heading, pitch, and bank), in the most continuous way possible? Specifically, how do I compute all equivalent Euler angle representations for a single rotation, and select the one that is 'closest' to a previous rotation in time, given the ambiguities and periodicities inherent in Euler angles? Are there systematic equivalence transformations, and what are their implications for continuity and numerical stability?
Mt_a:
1. Consider whether Euler angles are required, as quaternions offer a more robust and continuous representation for rotations, especially when comparing or interpolating between orientations.
2. With Euler angles, continuity can be improved by allowing the angles to range over all real numbers, rather than restricting them to a principal interval. This means treating the parameter space as $\mathbb{R}^3$ instead of $(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$.
3. There are several equivalence transformations for Euler angles:
   a. The obvious equivalence: adding multiples of $2\pi$ to any angle yields the same rotation.
   b. A less obvious equivalence: the transformation $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \rightarrow (\alpha+\pi, \pi-\beta, \gamma+\pi)$ also produces the same rotation, which is why $\beta$ is typically limited to an interval of length $\pi$.
   c. A third equivalence arises when $\beta \equiv 0 \pmod{\pi/2}$, where $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ apply to the same axis and their sum can be changed without affecting the rotation. This is rare unless $\beta$ is near these special values, but can cause numerical issues.
4. All equivalent Euler angle representations can be generated by combining these transformations.
5. To achieve continuity, select the equivalent representation that is closest (in Euclidean distance) to the previous set of angles.
Ra_a: To represent rotation curves as continuously as possible using Euler angles, allow the angles to range freely over $\mathbb{R}$ and use the known equivalence transformations (adding multiples of $2\pi$, the $(\alpha+\pi, \pi-\beta, \gamma+\pi)$ transformation, and special cases when $\beta \equiv 0$) to generate all equivalent representations. Then, select the representation closest to the previous one in time. However, for greater numerical stability and simplicity, consider using quaternions instead of Euler angles.
Rq_b: What are the precise equivalence relations among Euler angle representations for a given rotation, especially regarding the third type of equivalence? How do these equivalences affect the continuity and uniqueness of Euler angle curves, and what are the correct conditions for when the third equivalence applies?
Mt_b:
1. There are multiple ways to represent the same rotation using Euler angles due to their inherent ambiguities.
2. The third equivalence, as previously described, is not always applicable; it specifically applies when $\beta \equiv \pi/2 \pmod{\pi}$, not $\beta \equiv 0$.
3. In these cases, $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ both apply to the same axis, and changing $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ in ways that keep $\alpha+\gamma$ (or $\alpha-\gamma$ when they apply in opposite directions) constant does not alter the rotation.
4. For arbitrary rotations, this special equivalence is rarely relevant, but it can cause numerical issues if $\beta$ approaches these values.
5. This is another reason why quaternions are often preferred for representing rotations.
Ra_b: The third equivalence among Euler angles applies only when $\beta \equiv \pi/2 \pmod{\pi}$, where $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ act on the same axis and their sum (or difference) can be changed without affecting the rotation. For most arbitrary rotations, this is not a concern, but it can cause numerical issues near these values, making quaternions a preferable alternative.
output_a:
Are you constrained to using Euler angles? If you can decide freely what representation to use,  quaternions  would be preferable. In that representation, it's very easy to find which of two quaternions representing a rotation (which differ only by a sign) is closer to a given one. 
 With Euler angles, if you want the representation to be continuous, you can let the angles range over  $\mathbb R$  instead of restricting them to a single (half-)period. However, choosing the nearest of the equivalent representations will then be more complicated than with quaternions. Quite generally, a lot of things that are nasty, complicated and potentially numerically unstable with Euler angles become nicer and easier when you use quaternions. 
 [ Edit in response to the comments: ] 
 There are three equivalences, one obvious, another less obvious and a third only applicable in certain circumstances. 
 The obvious one is that you can always add multiples of  $2\pi$  to any of the angles; if you let them range over  $\mathbb R$ , which you must if you want to get continuous curves, this corresponds to using  $\mathbb R^3$  as the parameter space instead of the quotient  $(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ . This equivalence is easy to handle since you can change the three angles independently, that is, if you change one of them by a multiple of  $2\pi$ , you directly get the same rotation without changing the other two parameters. 
 What's less obvious is that (referring to  this image ) the transformation  $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\rightarrow(\alpha+\pi,\pi -\beta,\gamma+\pi)$  leads to the same rotation. (This is why, in order to get unique angles,  $\beta$  has to be limited to an interval of length  $\pi$ , not  $2\pi$ .) 
 A third equivalence comes into play only if  $\beta\equiv0\pmod{\pi/2}$ , since in this case  $\alpha$  and  $\gamma$  apply to the same axis and changing  $\alpha+\gamma$  doesn't change the rotation. If your rotations are arbitrary and have no reason to have  $\beta\equiv0$ , you won't need to consider this case, though it may cause numerical problems if you get close to  $\beta\equiv0$  (which is one good reason to use quaternions instead of Euler angles). 
 These three transformations generate all values of the Euler angles that are equivalent to each other. Remember that you also have to consider combinations of them, e.g. you can add multiples of  $2\pi$  in  $(\alpha+\pi,-\beta,\gamma+\pi)$  to get further equivalent angles.
